note: Launch conditions can now fetch the day's weather. ☁ Get weather, in the Launch panel and on the phone Fly screen, fetches one hour's weather for one place from Open-Meteo - the temperature, the station pressure at the pad's own altitude rather than a sea-level figure, and the 10 m wind, with the place's latitude and longitude - shows it beside what the panel holds, and writes only the rows you tick, when you press Apply. It also offers the ground height there, from Open-Meteo's terrain model, as the Site altitude, and while Site altitude is still 0 that choice starts selected, so Apply writes it unless you switch it off. A place name you search for, the chosen place's coordinates, the dates around the day you pick and the altitudes to fetch the air for go to Open-Meteo; nothing about your rocket does. Dates more than 92 days back come from Open-Meteo's historical archive, the weather as it was rather than a forecast: the ERA5 reanalysis, which Open-Meteo blends with ECMWF's 9 km IFS model for dates since 2017. It needs a connection. Weather data by Open-Meteo.com, CC BY 4.0. A density-altitude readout shows how thin the pad's air is - 7,122 ft at a 4,000 ft field on a 95 °F day. Once a forecast's wind is applied, a row offers an estimate of Wind gusts σ from the forecast gust, written only when you click it. A new Rod aim field says which way a tilted rod leans relative to the wind; 0°, into the wind, is how every flight flew before. And a new Longitude field travels with the .ork; it moves no flight number, only the Longitude column of the flight-data download. On the 1,069 design files the app is checked against, every one of the 768 that fly came out with the same numbers, except that 16 files' own longitude now shows, in the Longitude field and in that column. One kind of file can now fly differently, though none of the 1,069 is one: a desktop .ork whose tilted rod has 'Always launch directly up-wind or down-wind' turned off and a rod direction other than the wind's now opens with that direction as its Rod aim and flies it, as desktop does. And the guide's claim that the simulator's gusts have a realistic frequency content is corrected: they last about half a second, where real gusts last many seconds.
